methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students frequently over-apply the "-ed" rule to irregular verbs related to accidents or mistakes, resulting in errors like "breaked", "falled", "losed", or "finded".

Solution: Group these specific verbs under an "Accidents and Mistakes" theme. By attaching these irregular past tense forms to strong emotional contexts (surprise, regret, relief) and a "bad day" narrative, students form stronger cognitive anchors for the correct spellings and pronunciations.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What went wrong?" → student answers using irregular accident verbs.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher provides pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb ("lose") → student says past form ("lost"), meaning, and 1 sentence ("I lost my pencil").
S2 pull-out: Give a scenario ("You dropped a glass"). Student responds using key verbs ("I broke the glass. It was an accident!").
S3 pull-out: Assess VC script fluency. Check for overgeneralization errors.

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs. Each has a card showing different missing items and accidents. They ask questions to solve the mystery of the bad day. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. Ensure they hide their cards.
Students ask the provided questions to complete the missing events.
Students produce: A fully solved sequence of events.
broke: Mime snapping a stick in half over the knee.
lost: Shrug shoulders and look around confused.
found: Point index finger up and smile brightly (like an idea bulb).
clumsy: Pretend to trip and stumble.

content: Jake was running in the corridor. He hit his knee on the table and fell down.

She brought a cold pack and put it on his knee.

On Saturday, Luna wanted to help her dad. Dad was building a birdhouse in the garden. "Can I help?" asked Luna. "Yes, but be careful," Dad said. Luna carried a box of nails. Suddenly, she tripped over a rock and fell! The box broke, and the nails fell in the grass. "Oh no! It was an accident. I am clumsy today," Luna cried. "Are you okay?" Dad asked. "Don't cry. We can fix it." Luna was sorry for the mistake. She looked in the green grass. After ten minutes, she found all the lost nails! Dad smiled and they built the birdhouse together. "Next time, I will be more careful," Luna promised.

content: Science: Materials and Why Some Things Break
Different materials have different properties — some are hard, some are soft, some are fragile:
• Glass: hard but FRAGILE (breaks easily)  • Plastic: hard but FLEXIBLE (doesn't break easily)
• Wood: strong but can split  • Rubber: stretchy and bouncy

listening_script.text: Poor Tom! Yesterday was a bad day! First, he fell out of bed. Ouch! Then, he broke his glasses. "Oh no! I broke them!" he said. His mom was not angry. "Accidents happen," she said. At school, Tom lost his pencil case. "I lost it! Where is it?" he looked everywhere. A friend found it under the desk. "I found your pencil case!" she said. "Thank you!" said Tom. At home, Tom broke a plate. "I am so sorry, Mom! I am clumsy today!" "Be more careful," said Mom. "But don't worry. We can fix it." Finally, Tom found his lost homework. It fell behind the bookshelf! "What a day!" said Tom.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance (do NOT share with students):

Student A: Names one accident from Tom's bad day (e.g., "Tom fell out of bed").
Student B: Names another (e.g., "He broke his glasses").
Goal: Use fell / broke correctly — two distinct accident verbs in past tense.

PULL-OUT TASK (S1):
— Show a 'bad day' illustration. Ask: "What happened to Tom first? What happened next?"
— Scaffold weaker students: "First, Tom ___ out of bed. Then, he ___ his glasses."
— Target elicitation: fell / broke — confirm students DON'T say 'falled' or 'breaked'.

COMMUNICATIVE TASK TIP:
— Model immediately: "We say FELL (not 'falled') and BROKE (not 'breaked')."
— Stronger students: add lost / found: "He also LOST his bag but FOUND it under the table."

teacher_contents.grammar_notes:
• break→broke, fall→fell, lose→lost, find→found — four accident and discovery verbs
• Paired opposites: lose ↔ find (two sides of the same event)
• Error prevention: 'breaked' ✗ → broke ✓ | 'falled' ✗ → fell ✓ | 'losed' ✗ → lost ✓ | 'founded' ✗ → found ✓
• Phonics note: 'found' rhymes with 'round/sound'; 'fell' rhymes with 'bell/well' — helps memory
• Narrative tip: these verbs often appear in sequence — 'He fell, then he broke, then he lost...'

listening_script.text: On Saturday, Luna wanted to help her dad. Dad was building a birdhouse in the garden. "Can I help?" asked Luna. "Yes, but be careful," Dad said. Luna carried a box of nails. Suddenly, she tripped over a rock and fell! The box broke, and the nails fell in the grass. "Oh no! It was an accident. I am clumsy today," Luna cried. "Are you okay?" Dad asked. "Don't cry. We can fix it." Luna was sorry for the mistake. She looked in the green grass. After ten minutes, she found all the lost nails! Dad smiled and they built the birdhouse together. "Next time, I will be more careful," Luna promised.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes what Luna was trying to do (e.g., "Luna wanted to help her dad build a birdhouse").
Student B: Names what went wrong (e.g., "She fell and broke a piece").
Goal: Use fell / broke / lost / found in a cause-and-effect sentence.

PULL-OUT TASK (S2):
— Ask: "What did Luna do wrong? What happened because of the accident?"
— Scaffold: "Luna was helping when she ___ and ___. Then, she ___."
— Error focus: 'lost' vs 'found' — pair them: "She LOST the hammer but FOUND it later."

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: timeline cards — put Luna's accident story in order.
— Stronger students: retell using all four verbs: "Luna fell, broke, lost, and finally found..."

Science: Materials and Breaking
[ALL] Read this: Why do some things break when they fall, but other things do not? It depends on the MATERIAL! Glass and ceramics are rigid (hard) but brittle. This means they break or shatter easily when they hit a hard floor. Rubber and plastic are flexible or bouncy. They can bend and absorb the shock of falling. If you are clumsy, it is better to use a plastic cup. It is safer!

listening_script.text: Max wrote a story for his English class. "Last week, I made a terrible mistake! I lost my mother's special ring. I looked in my room. I looked in the kitchen. I was so worried. I told my mom, 'I am so sorry. I lost your ring. It was an accident.' Mom was sad, but she said, 'We will find it.' The next day, I helped my dad fix his car in the garage. A small shiny thing fell from the car seat. It fell onto the floor. I looked closely. I found the ring! I ran to my mom and gave it to her. She was so happy. I was not clumsy this time. I was a great detective!"
dictation: I found it on the floor.

teacher_contents.speaking_notes:
SPEAKING CHECKPOINT — Teacher Guidance:

Student A: Describes Max's biggest mistake (e.g., "Max lost his mother's watch").
Student B: Continues with what happened next (e.g., "He found it under the sofa").
Goal: W33 mastery — broke / fell / lost / found in a narrative retell.

PULL-OUT TASK (S3 — Communicative Task):
— Ask: "Tell me Max's whole accident story — what did he lose? What did he break? What did he find?"
— Target retell: "Max LOST the watch. He FELL when he was looking. He BROKE a cup. Finally, he FOUND it."
— Mastery check: all four verbs fluently used with sequence words.

DIFFERENTIATION:
— Weaker students: "Name ONE thing Max lost and ONE thing he found."
— Stronger students: write a 4-sentence accident story using all four verbs.

Health/Safety: Preventing Accidents
[ALL] Read this: Accidents happen, but we can prevent them! Being careful means thinking before we act. If you run on a wet floor, you might slip and fall. The cause is running on water, and the effect is falling! If you carry too many glass cups, you might drop them. They will break. To be safe, we must walk slowly and use two hands. Being careful protects our body and our things!
